subject: capybara
pitch:
Category: Animal.
Subject: capybara with a small bird on its head.
Style: whimsical.
reasoning:
I'm planning out a whimsical capybara illustration in a resting pose, thinking through its proportions—barrel body, boxy head, small ears, sleepy eyes—with a tiny bird perched on its head, along with a skeleton study for anatomical accuracy.

Now I'm working through the joint hierarchy: hips as root, spine chain from hips to chest using catmull points, then neck and head joints with proper positioning, plus four legs, ears, tail stub, and the bird's own skeleton (body, wings, tail, beak). I'm calculating specific coordinates for body length, height, and head placement to get the proportions right.

Writing muzzle and body sweep geometry...

For coloring, I'm planning mottled brown fur tones with countershading so the belly reads lighter than the back, plus some grain detail for streaky fur texture. Then I'm sketching short stubby legs as limb segments running from hip to foot with small length values to keep the stance low.

Now I'm working through limb bending—front legs bend elbows backward, hind legs bend knees forward—and chaining joints from shoulder to elbow to hand (or hip to knee to foot), parented appropriately to the spine or hips. I'm adding sweep radii for the leg thickness, then shaping feet as flattened spheres with a few small toe parts attached to the tip joint for a simple paw-like look.

For the head I'm planning dark sphere eyes with tiny white highlight spheres, droopy half-sphere lids for a sleepy look, and flattened pink sphere discs for whimsical blush on the cheeks, all attached as parts on the skull.

Placing the skull sphere, then shaping the muzzle as a tapered frustum extending forward, with a small dark nose pad positioned at the tip and nostrils facing forward and up. Below that I'm adding the jaw as a box offset downward and forward from a joint point to complete the lower face structure.

Still defining joint hierarchy and ear placement...

For eyes, I need to position them on the skull's surface rather than guessing coordinates — I'm computing the ellipsoid check and realizing my test point falls inside the skull, so I should use a proper surface-projection function based on spherical direction angles to place the eyes correctly on the skull surface.

Switching to a surface-hit approach using azimuth and elevation, placing eyes, ears, and cheek blush discs by querying the skull's surface at specific angles, then sticking appropriately-sized spheres and flattened discs onto those hit points with matching colors and embed depth.

For the eyes themselves, I'm switching strategy to decals instead of sphere stacking—drawing a whimsical sleepy/happy eye as an SVG texture with a dark iris, big highlight, lid line, and lashes, applied as a mirrored decal oriented along the hit normal, letting the surrounding fur show through transparency.

Now I'm planning a small bluebird perched on top of the head, positioning its body joint just above the skull's top surface and sketching out its basic proportions before building its joint hierarchy.

Still working out the bird's build...

Settling on scale [0.03,0.055,0.012] so the wing is thin vertically and wide front-to-back, then working out the tail as a similarly flattened wedge pointing back and slightly up. I'm planning legs as thin orange rods down to the feet, a few small cones for the head crest, and setting up the joint hierarchy with body parenting head, figuring out the body-to-skull height placement.

Now I'm settling on the bird's color palette -- blue body, cream belly, darker blue wings, orange beak -- and considering countershading on the body sphere. For the capybara, I'm adding a small nub tail, a few thin whisker rods per side near the muzzle, and thinking about fur tufts via small cards on the body.

I'm scattering brown tuft cards across the upper body surface for texture, tinted with a warm brown, and now working out the fur paint using a mottled countershade with subtle brightness variation.

For shading, I'm making the head slightly darker on top with a lighter muzzle and darker legs/feet via a vertical gradient from the main fur color to a dark brown. I'm also checking body sweep proportions so the belly sits low and legs stay short, matching a capybara's stocky build.

Now I'm refining the leg joint positions so the hip-to-foot reach matches the leg segment lengths, then placing small ellipsoid feet with three dark rounded toe nubs at the front of each foot for detail.

For bones, I'm attaching each chain to its last joint, naming the front limbs shoulder/elbow/wrist and the hind limbs hip/knee/ankle with L/R suffixes, and parenting the shoulders to the nearest spine joint.

Now I'm tuning the spine extent and body radius so the rear looks thick and rounded like a capybara, shrinking the radius smoothly near both ends so the round caps taper naturally instead of ballooning.

Still shaping the neck sweep...

Now I'm attaching the skull sphere to the head bone with proper scale, then moving on to blocking out the muzzle shape with a frustum box.

Working out the muzzle dimensions against the skull geometry to make sure the proportions line up at the jaw line and mouth position.

Now I'm adding the nose pad as a small sphere near the top-front of the muzzle with tiny black nostril spheres embedded, then setting up thin dark whisker rods angled outward from the muzzle sides in sets of three.

For the cheeks, I'm placing blush discs onto the skull at a forward-facing azimuth and slightly downward elevation, checking that the muzzle doesn't block them. For the ears, I'm positioning squashed sphere shapes at the back-top of the skull, flattening them along the stick's local axis to get a disc-like ear shape.

I'm now adjusting the ear geometry so it pokes outward and upward rather than lying flat, scaling the sphere to be taller along the normal direction and narrower in depth, then adding a smaller pink inner-ear shape nested slightly inside using the same local coordinate frame.

I'm skipping the inner-pink complexity for now since the z-direction orientation is unreliable, and settling on a simpler dark-tinted ear color instead. For the eyes, I'm sketching an SVG decal with a dark ellipse, a highlight, a lid arc, and small lashes, then figuring out placement angles on the skull ellipsoid relative to the muzzle.

Checking the math, the eye position at azimuth 62 risks overlapping the muzzle box since both are near the same x and z coordinates at that surface point, so I'm narrowing the muzzle width and widening the skull slightly, then recalculating eye placement at azimuth 55 to keep it clear of the muzzle's half-width.

Moving the eyes further back to azimuth 68-70 degrees keeps them safely outside the muzzle region now. I'm setting up the decal direction logic, then placing a small bird figure on top of the skull/hat with a body, head sphere, eye spheres, and a cone-shaped beak.

Still positioning beak cones...

Now I'm setting up the bird's joint hierarchy (body, head, beak, wings, tail) and placing tiny leg rods and toe discs in orange on the body, plus a countershaded belly sphere and small crest cones on the head.

Adjusting wing position and direction for a resting pose, keeping the half-length shorter so the spread isn't too wide relative to the body, and adding a darker smaller sphere near the tip for feather contrast.

For the capybara, I'm reconsidering the spine length along the z-axis—shrinking it from an overly long 1.5m span down closer to the realistic 1.0-1.3m range by pulling in the neck and rear dome positions while keeping head and tail proportions sensible.

Now I'm working out leg joint placements: front legs with shoulder and foot positions along z and y, hind legs set slightly more bent with hip and foot points, choosing bone lengths and bend hints (elbow back for front, knee forward for hind) to make the two-bone IK solve naturally for a chubby, stocky stance.

Both leg parents can use nearestJoint lookup against the spine. For fur, I'm scattering tuft-shaped cards across the body surface with randomized size, lean, and bend, tinting them a grey-brown to blend with the body gradient, relying on default flow direction and the rng seed helper for randomization.

I'll add a smaller cheek ruff by scattering fewer tuft cards around the skull with tighter spacing, keeping whimsical extras minimal—no musical notes or daisies, just a soft blush and open eyes to keep the character simple. I'm pulling hit points from the skull surface around a center point to place these, then finalizing the texture set with just eye and tuft materials.

Now I'm writing a helper function to safely handle null surface hits, placing pink cylinder discs for cheeks, and assigning jaw roles to the mouth parts. I'm also verifying the model's bounding box sits flush at y=0 and finalizing the metadata export before writing the full code.
